name: Marco Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to employers, AI companies or government. This conversation is confidential, and there is no right answer. What is a normal day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach drums after school, record percussion for a small game studio and lead a weekend band. I’m 27, have a music master’s and can hear when a pattern is a fraction late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A pupil finding the backbeat without staring at me makes the long day worthwhile. Hauling a kit upstairs and wondering whether the studio will pay on Friday are the parts I would gladly skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my rehearsal band AI Plateau leaves the Tuesday set and weekend drum lessons alone. A quicker invoice is useful, though I still want to know who signed the booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income is fairly steady across school lessons, small recording jobs and the band. I have about four months of expenses saved, so a weak recording week would not put the rent at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my six drum pupils and the band’s booked dates. I’d use the simple calendar tool I already know for lesson reminders, but I would check each invoice myself before sending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my own work. A quiet week would be irritating, but it would not make me cancel a lesson or call my parents for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where is the main time lost now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Packing and setting up the kit takes longer than sending an invoice. No screen is going to carry my bass drum up the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new gear with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old kit works, and my four-month reserve is for missed work. I would replace a broken head from paid gig money.

say: I’d tell the band **Tuesday sets** and weekend drum lessons still need players and pupils.
I’d accept a quicker **invoice** while keeping human sign-off on paid bookings.
think: Six **pupils** and booked sets keep my income fairly steady.
A **four-month reserve** can cover a weak recording week without changing my rent plan.
do: Keep six **drum pupils** and all booked band dates on the calendar.
Check each **invoice** before sending it through the familiar reminder tool.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and rent, though a quiet week would still annoy me.
fieldNote: He distinguishes a modest **calendar saving** from the physical setup that takes most of his time.
His **reserve** stays for missed work; he will not buy new equipment simply because he can.
S0.quote: No screen is going to carry my bass drum up the stairs.

steps.text: Keep six drum pupils and booked band dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band Steady Disruption could cut the simple rhythm tracks I record for small games. I would still expect live sets and one-to-one lessons to take time for people to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the game studio may ask for fewer takes or lower rates. That work covers my practice room rent, so losing it would make me rework the week even with four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio this month which recordings it still plans to commission at a paid rate. If its fees fall in the first year, I’d spend one afternoon learning how a colleague checks generated drum parts, then offer one extra school lesson only if a room and pupil open up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the studio money, but I have time to check one thing at a time. A cheap beat can fill a game, but it cannot loosen a child’s stiff wrist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What rate would make the recording worth doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording rate has to cover travel and the practice room. I would ask for that number in writing before taking more tracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI now and then; what would you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI for rough schedules, not drum audio. A colleague could teach me to spot a bad generated pattern before a client hears it.

say: I’d warn the band that **simple game tracks** may draw fewer paid recording calls.
I’d ask the studio to confirm **rates** before I record more parts.
think: Studio **fees** pay my practice room rent, so a cut would force a weekly change.
Live **sets** and one-to-one lessons might last longer, but I would not treat them as guaranteed.
do: Ask the game **studio** this month which tracks still carry a paid rate covering travel and room.
Learn to check generated **drum audio** with a colleague if fees fall; add a lesson only with a pupil and room.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the studio rent, though my savings let me check options.
fieldNote: He uses AI for **schedules**, so checking generated drum audio would be a genuinely new skill.
He sets a **paid-rate** floor and makes the extra lesson depend on a vacancy and pupil.
S1.quote: A cheap beat can fill a game, but it cannot loosen a child’s stiff wrist.

steps.text: Ask studio for paid track rates covering travel and room
Learn to check generated drum audio with colleague if fees fall
Add school drum lesson if fees fall and pupil and room open

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band AGI by 2028 could take the planning and recording work quickly, with capable robots for hands-on playing around 2031. I would not tell pupils the drum stool is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio could stop paying me within two years, and schools could buy AI lessons too. Four months of expenses would help for a short gap, not replace a career if both parts collapsed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the school now how many lesson hours are contracted and ask the studio for its next paid dates. If recording ends in the first year after 2028, I’d give notice on the practice room within the lease terms and apply for a posted school teaching vacancy at a clear rate. I would keep my six current pupils until a paid offer exists, and ask my parents for a short stay only if my reserve runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because the studio work could vanish before I have replacement hours. If school lessons collapsed too, I would be alarmed. The 2028 studio phone going quiet frightens me before any robot drummer walks in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do before giving up the room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the lease notice first and move rehearsals to the school only if it allowed that use. Breaking a contract would not make a sensible one-year saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my parents I am applying for teaching work, not asking them to cover rent now. If my reserve ran out, I would ask whether I could stay briefly.

say: I’d tell players **recording and planning** face AGI in 2028, before capable performance robots around 2031.
I would tell pupils the **drum stool** is not guaranteed work forever.
think: The **studio** and school could both cut paid hours in a fast change.
Four months of **savings** cover a gap, not a lasting loss of both incomes.
do: Check contracted **school hours** and paid studio dates now; keep six pupils until a paid offer exists.
Give **practice-room notice** if recording stops after 2028 and the lease allows; apply for a posted vacancy at clear pay.
Ask my **parents** for a brief stay only if my four-month reserve runs out.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing studio income, and I would be alarmed if school hours also collapsed.
fieldNote: He places the near threat in **2028 recording work**, with capable robots for physical playing around 2031.
He checks **lease terms** and requires a posted paid vacancy rather than counting on a nonexistent teaching job.
S2.quote: The 2028 studio phone going quiet frightens me before any robot drummer walks in.

steps.text: Keep six pupils while checking contracted school hours and paid studio dates
Give practice-room notice if recording stops after 2028 and lease allows
Apply for posted paid school vacancy if recording stops; keep pupils until offer
Ask parents for short stay only if four-month reserve runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 leaves five years to watch the studio market. Robots able to handle the playing itself would arrive around 2034, so I would use that gap for teaching, not declare gigs safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save from paid studio work while it lasts and get better at checking machine-made audio. I still think the studio may cut rates before 2031, and I do not know how many parents will keep buying lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I’d ask a producer to let me sit in on one paid track check, with permission to use a copy that contains no client material. If that check proves useful, I’d teach one short workshop next summer only if the school approves it and six people pay for the room and my time. In the first year after 2031, I would repeat it only if school approval and six paid seats still cover both costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years gives me room to learn without gambling the reserve. I can test a class and walk away if nobody pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why six people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six paid seats make a workshop; five seats make me a volunteer with a room bill. The school room and my afternoon both need paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the producer says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep playing and ask another producer for a safe demonstration. I will not upload a client’s private track to practise.

say: I’d tell the band **2031 AGI** leaves time to see studio demand before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would focus on **teaching** without promising that gigs stay safe.
think: Paid **studio work** can build savings while it lasts.
I cannot assume **parents** will keep buying lessons once AI teaching improves.
do: Ask a producer for one **safe track-checking session** using permitted material this winter.
Offer a **workshop** with school approval and six paid seats covering room and time; repeat after 2031 only under those conditions.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough time to test a class without spending the reserve.
fieldNote: He seeks permission and avoids uploading **client material**, preserving a real safe-use condition.
The workshop needs **school approval** and six fees that cover both the room and his afternoon.
S3.quote: Six paid seats make a workshop; five seats make me a volunteer with a room bill.

steps.text: Learn audio checking from producer using permitted nonclient material
Offer workshop with school approval and six paid seats covering room and time
Repeat workshop after 2031 only with school approval and six paid seats covering room and time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my band AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make choices, though thinking work still changes then. Capable robots for hands-on playing would come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I would want a larger teaching roster and a reserve beyond four months, if the work stays paid. A weekly café gig is a fine Saturday, but a poor ten-year budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the school for written renewal dates this year and save a set part of each studio payment after rent and tax. In the first year after 2036, I’d review the real lesson list before committing to a bigger room or another kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about the long future, not desperate tonight. I have some work nearby to apply for and enough savings to change course if bookings thin out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with ten from each paid studio track and raise it only after the reserve reaches six months of bills. I would count paid tracks, not promised ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop performing to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the band and it pays, so I would not stop performing today. I would change the balance only after a school offered actual hours at a clear rate.

say: I’d tell the band a **decade** allows planning before thinking AGI in 2036.
I would remind them capable **playing robots** could arrive around 2039.
think: A larger **teaching roster** could make my income steadier if the hours are paid.
I will not build a ten-year budget on a **weekly café gig**.
do: Ask the school for written **renewal dates** this year and keep paid band work.
Save **ten** from each paid studio track after rent and tax; review lesson demand before new space after 2036.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later change, with savings and nearby openings giving me some control.
fieldNote: He treats the **decade** as time to collect real hours and savings, not a guarantee of demand.
He will not buy **space or gear** against projected lessons before checking the actual roster.
S4.quote: A weekly café gig is a fine Saturday, but a poor ten-year budget.

steps.text: Ask school for written renewal dates and keep paid band work
Save ten from each paid studio track after rent and tax

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because studio fees might stop before my teaching week grows. A posted school vacancy at a clear rate and room access for lessons would help if the present studio work ends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked whether I would still play for fun if nobody hired me. I would. Pleasure does not cover rent, and I want to keep the two accounts separate.

headlineQuote: Pleasure does not cover rent, and I want to keep the two accounts separate.
portrait: At **27**, Marco leads a band, records percussion and teaches six drum pupils after a music master’s degree.
His typical **pay** and four-month reserve cushion a short gap, while studio fees cover practice-room rent.
He uses AI for **schedules** sometimes and would learn audio checking only with safe, permitted material.
The fast **2028** case threatens studio fees first; he seeks a paid school opening before changing jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end studio fees before his school teaching week grows.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **school vacancy** at a clear rate and approved lesson space would help replace lost studio work.
